https://telex.hu/gazdasag/2026/09/19/mag.text: Menü Kereső Magyar Péter Mészáros Lőrincnek: Orbán Viktor strómanja rosszul méri fel a helyzetet Gazdaság Az MKIF által kezelt M1-es autópálya felújítási munkálatai miatti útterelés az Óbarok lehajtónál 2025. szeptember 22-én – Fotó: Kocsis Zoltán / MTI Molnár Zoltán Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „Mészáros Lőrincék máris jogászokkal fenyegetőznek, miután tegnap bejelentettük, hogy az állam nem fogja továbbvinni az előző hatalom által nekik kijátszott, felfoghatatlan méretű 23 ezer milliárd forintos mutyit” – közölte a Facebookon szombaton Magyar Péter miniszterelnök. Magyar a „23 ezer milliárd forintos mutyin” az autópályák jelentős részének koncessziós üzemeltetését értette, ami az állam szerint csak bizonyos üzleti köröket gazdagított. Mint megírtuk , a kormány döntést hozott arról pénteken, hogy elindítja a 2022-ben indult, 35 éves, Mészáros-féle autópálya-koncesszió megszüntetését szolgáló lépéseket. Közölték, a döntésről pénteken tájékoztatják a koncessziós céget, és megkezdik velük a tárgyalást a tevékenységük lezárásáról. Vitézy Dávid közlekedési és beruházási miniszter akkor azt mondta, nem akarnak évekig tartó jogvitát, ezért akarnak tárgyalni, és közös megegyezéssel kijönni az egészből. A kormányfő Facebook-posztja szerint ez a tárgyalás nehézkes lesz, az MKIF Magyar Koncessziós Infrastruktúra Fejlesztő Zrt. jogi útra terelheti a dolgot. „Szerintem Orbán Viktor strómanja rosszul méri fel a helyzetet, miközben a pénzünkön vett francia pezsgőt leöblíti egy dobozos kávéval” – üzent Magyar Péter a cég tulajdonosának, majd hosszas posztban, rengeteg példával igyekezett érzékeltetni, milyen sok pénz is 23 billió forint. Például annyi, hogy ha a „20 ezer forintos címletekben egymásra tennénk őket, akkor kb. 138 km magas oszlopot kapnánk. Ez 15-ször magasabb lenne, mint a Mount Everest.” Magyar végül megkérte Mészáros feleségét, Várkonyi Andreát, hogy olvassa fel az üzenetet a címzettnek. A miniszterelnök posztjából az következik, hogy az MKIF a jogi utat választhatja, bár a társaság egy napja még annyit közölt csak: „A Társaság várja, hogy a bejelentésnek megfelelően a kormányzat megküldje számára a hivatalos, írásos tájékoztatást. Az MKIF Zrt. ennek megismerését követően alakítja ki hivatalos álláspontját, amelyről a későbbiekben tájékoztatja a nyilvánosságot.” Mindennek feloldásában segíthet Vitézy Dávid szombat kora reggeli Facebook -bejegyzése. A közlekedési és beruházási miniszter mellékelt egy dokumentumrészletet, amit Németh Tamás, az MKIF vezérigazgatója írt alá. Ebben összetett jogi megfogalmazásban voltaképp arról ír, hogy az állami kifejezett vagy ráutaló magatartása, nyilatkozata arról, hogy érvényes, hatályos, semmis lehet-e a koncessziós szerződés, alkalmas rá, hogy a koncessziót finanszírozók magatartását hátrányosan befolyásolja. „A finanszírozással összefüggően bekövetkező hátrányos jogkövetkezmények kapcsán a vonatkozó jogszabályok és a Koncessziós Szerződés alapján a koncessziós jogosultak az őket megillető valamennyi jogukat és igényüket kifejezetten fenntartják” – zárta mondandóját Németh. Tehát az MKIF akár jogi útra is terelheti az ügyet e szerint. „Erőltetett jogászkodás és erőtlen fenyegetőzés – ennyire tellett Mészárosék autópálya-koncesszorától” – kommentálta a vezérigazgató levelét Vitézy. Hozzátette: „Szeretném egyértelműen és nyilvánosan is rögzíteni: akár a jogi fenyegetőzés és a magyar emberek elleni pereskedés útját, akár a kárenyhítő közreműködés útját választják, a 23 ezer milliárd forintnak búcsút mondhatnak. Vége van.” Vitézy korábban azt mondta , az lenne az ideális, ha az MKIF a következő hónapokban átadná a feladatai elvégzéséhez szükséges eszközöket, és már idén december 31-gyel kilépne ebből a feladatból. Az autópálya-hálózat működtetése ezzel a kormány tervei szerint ahhoz a Magyar Közúthoz kerülne vissza, ami ezt a feladatot a koncessziós szerződés megkötése előtt is végezte. A Magyar Közút azonban a koncessziós szerződés 2022-es megkötésekor az autópálya-mérnökségeket beleértve a teljes eszközállományát átadta az MKIF-nek, így a feladat visszaadásához ezt vissza kellene adniuk. A kormány azért is szeretné szerződésbontás helyett tárgyalással lezárni a koncessziót, hogy ezt az eszközállományt a lehető leghamarabb és gördülékenyebb módon visszaszerezzék. Magyar Péter már a kampányban megígérte, hogy hatalomra jutásuk esetén felmondják a Mészárosékkal kötött koncessziós szerződést. A konkrét lépés kidolgozása a májusi kormányalakítás után Vitézy Dávid közlekedési és beruházási miniszternek jutott, aki többször megerősítette, hogy erre készülnek. Az előző kormány még 2021-ben adta ki 35 évre – a 2022 és 2057 közötti időszakra – a magyar autópálya-hálózat nagy részét a Mészáros Lőrinc és Szíjj László tulajdonában lévő Magyar Koncessziós Infrastruktúra Fejlesztő (MKIF) Zrt.-nek. A koncessziós vállalat feladata az lenne, hogy több mint nettó 20 ezer milliárd forintért végezze az érintett pályaszakaszok karbantartását, bővítse azok egy részét és a szerződés értelmében új autópályákat is építsen. A szerződés lehetővé teszi azt, hogy a Mészáros Lőrinc és Szíjj László tulajdonában lévő MKIF közbeszerzés nélkül Mészáros és Szíjj saját cégeit, Orbán Győző bányavállalatát, esetleg Várkonyi Andrea kommunikációs cégét bízza meg a munkák elvégzésével. A koncesszió miatt az Európai Bizottság már 2024-ben indított egy kötelezettségszegési eljárást, amelyben több ponton kritizálták a koncessziós modellt. Recent moves build on power limit reforms and licensing changes favoring faster deployment. Competition remains open while interference disputes with rivals continue. Starship tests promise even greater scale. FCC’s Spectrum Giveaway Sets Stage for Starlink’s Next Leap Written by Victoria Mossi Saturday, September 12, 2026 The Federal Communications Commission stands ready to hand satellite operators a fresh 1,050 MHz of spectrum. A vote scheduled for Sept. 30 could reshape broadband delivery from homes to airplanes and ships. SpaceX’s Starlink sits at the center of these changes. Yet the rules won’t favor any single player. Regulators plan to open the 12.7-13.25 GHz band for 550 MHz and the 42.0-42.5 GHz band for 500 MHz. The spectrum would support consumer connections, earth stations in motion, inter-satellite links and traffic routing through fixed ground stations. Reuters first detailed the proposal on Sept. 8. FCC Chair Brendan Carr described the move plainly. “The changes will not only make a difference here on Earth, but also in the skies above.” Additional capacity for links between satellites would strengthen network resilience. It would improve service to ships, planes and vehicles. New industrial applications in space could follow. Big bets. Higher stakes. This isn’t isolated action. The FCC eased power limits on satellite spectrum in April. That adjustment alone promised to lift capacity between 100% and 700% without adding more satellites. Economic gains could exceed $2 billion. Starlink gained breathing room then. Now it stands to gain more. The company already operates thousands of low-Earth orbit satellites. It serves millions of subscribers worldwide. Direct-to-cell capabilities have expanded through partnerships with carriers like T-Mobile. But competition looms. The new spectrum remains open to all qualified operators. Success will hinge on who secures approvals and deploys equipment fast enough. Viasat, Eutelsat’s OneWeb and others watch closely. SpaceX has tangled with rivals before. It petitioned the FCC in August to block Viasat’s next satellite over interference fears. PCMag covered the dispute. Coordination talks dragged. Interference risks in shared bands remain real. Meanwhile the agency eyes even more spectrum. Another 1,450 MHz in Ku- and Ka-bands plus 138.25 GHz in the D-band could open later. CircleID reported these details on Sept. 11. The moves build on licensing reforms adopted in July. Those changes cut approval times from years to weeks. A so-called licensing assembly line now speeds deployment of next-generation systems. Starlink’s ambitions stretch further. The company acquired 65 MHz of mid-band spectrum from EchoStar earlier this year for direct-to-device service. FCC approval of that deal in May unlocked new paths. SpaceX told investors it eyes a retail mobile offering in the U.S. that could challenge traditional carriers. AT&T’s CEO recently weighed in on the threat during a Goldman Sachs conference. Yahoo Finance captured his comments on Sept. 10. Disruption talk fills boardrooms. Yet satellite signals struggle indoors and in dense cities. Engineering hurdles persist. International deals add momentum. Hungarian group 4iG signed agreements with SpaceX for Starlink mobile rollout across Hungary and parts of the Western Balkans. First-generation service targets LTE phones without special terminals. A 5G non-terrestrial follow-on is planned. Service could begin in 2027. CircleID outlined the partnership on Sept. 11. Regulatory approvals in each market will decide timing. Starship tests promise to accelerate everything. SpaceX prepares Flight 14 for mid-September. It could carry the first V3 Starlink satellites to real orbit. The massive rocket’s success would lower launch costs further. Higher performance satellites would follow. Investors track these developments. SpaceX’s valuation rests heavily on Starlink’s growth. Recent reports suggest the network now exceeds 10 million subscribers. Environmental concerns shadow the expansion. Astronomers worry about light pollution and atmospheric effects from thousands more satellites. The FCC moved in early September to exempt satellite constellations from certain environmental reviews. Chairman Carr called outdated rules a drag on builders. Critics argue the agency underestimates long-term impacts. Ozone damage from deorbiting satellites draws particular scrutiny. Domestic politics enter the picture too. Some lawmakers question heavy reliance on a single provider for critical connectivity. Rural broadband programs have drawn fire. SpaceX once argued the $4.5 billion high-cost fund had become unnecessary because Starlink already solved access gaps. The debate continues. Yet the trajectory looks clear. Regulators favor faster innovation in space-based systems. Spectrum abundance supports that goal. Starlink holds first-mover advantages in scale, launch cadence and vertical integration. Its satellites are designed and built in-house. Compliance teams wrestle with FCC, ISED, ETSI and global rules daily. Interference fights will intensify. So will coordination demands. The April power limit changes replaced rigid restrictions with performance-based protections. That shift favored aggressive operators. SpaceX pushed the boundaries. Rivals cried foul. The pattern repeats with each new band. Consumers stand to benefit if capacity grows and prices fall. Remote areas gain options. Aviation and maritime sectors see reliability improvements. Emergency response gets another tool. Spain activated Starlink direct-to-device during recent wildfires. Similar uses emerged after earthquakes in Venezuela. The Sept. 30 vote marks another step. Not the last. Further proposals on unlicensed spectrum for direct-to-device devices are already circulating. The FCC seeks comments through November. Flexible rules could spur more experimentation. SpaceX doesn’t wait. Starship development continues. New satellite generations roll out. Global partnerships multiply. The company’s focus on spectrum, launches and technology integration positions it for dominance. Regulators appear willing to clear paths. But they stop short of picking winners. The market will test who can deliver. And the skies keep filling. Signals keep multiplying. Connectivity reaches farther than before. The question now becomes how far, how fast and at what cost to other priorities in orbit and on the ground. Subscribe for Updates SpaceRevolution Newsletter Notice an error? https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crkg.text: Image source, AFP Image caption, The China-flagged container shipping vessel Hui Fa off Khor Fakkan, in the Gulf of Oman, on Tuesday By David Gritten Published 5 hours ago A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities. All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said. Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz. The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water. The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday. Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added. Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February. At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization. The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time. However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency. One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters. To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Russia's foreign minister Sergei Lavrov attends the first plenary session at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, on Friday. Photograph: Peter Zay/Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Russia's foreign minister Sergei Lavrov attends the first plenary session at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, on Friday. Photograph: Peter Zay/Anadolu/Getty Images Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Russia Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Moscow’s Lavrov snubbed at G20 in Atlanta Russian foreign minister heavily criticised by EU foreign policy chief, and plans for the traditional ‘family photo’ abandoned. What we know on day 1,711 Guardian staff and agencies Sat 31 Oct 2026 00.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The EU’s foreign policy chief has accused Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov of presenting “lies” in G20 meetings in Atlanta about the Ukrainian conflict and suggested Moscow was not ready for peace negotiations . “We were talking about the big geopolitical crisis, including Ukraine, and we were able to address Sergei Lavrov head-on with this,” Kaja Kallas told Agence France-Presse on the sidelines of a meeting on Friday. “Of course, he put forward a lot of lies, a lot of false narratives that we were also able to then rebuke.” Kallas said Russia did not appear ready to move ahead in peace talks. “Even if they would have said this in words, their deeds tell something else,” she said. “July, August, and September have been the deadliest months for civilians in Ukraine.” She added: “They should show with their deeds that they are ready to negotiate, but they are clearly, clearly not.” At the talks, which are focusing on global economic growth, energy security and trade, European officials pushed Russia to secure a ceasefire in the Black Sea, an important agriculture export corridor . However, Lavrov conceded no ground on Ukraine and at a press conference, he criticised Europeans for their “arrogant boycott” while praising the willingness of US President Donald Trump’s administration to engage with Moscow. Plans for a traditional family photo of G20 ministers were called off after some European officials objected to appearing alongside Lavrov . Moscow has been shunned by most of the West since it invaded Ukraine, and Lavrov himself remains under international sanctions. The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said: “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years.” German foreign minister Johann Wadephul said there would be no photo because “there is no normality with Russia”. US secretary of state Marco Rubio spoke briefly with Lavrov on the sidelines of the G20 meeting , with the Russian minister saying both sides had a “decent talk”. Trump has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to Florida in December and has eased some sanctions on Moscow while touting a deal for Russia to sell diesel as prices soared. The Russian foreign minister’s G20 appearance comes also ahead of fresh negotiations expected between Moscow, Kyiv and Washington in November. Meanwhile, the Trump administration on Friday approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1bn , the state department said, but Ukraine’s president has warned deliveries could take years . The approval, which goes to Congress for review, comes after weeks of complaints by Ukrainian authorities that its supplies of the interceptor missiles were dwindling. A state department statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered but Volodymyr Zelenskyy said late Friday in a post on X that “deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS”. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles – which are yet to be manufactured – are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s. Patriot missiles are among the most important weapons Ukraine has to intercept Russian drones and missiles. The Ukrainian president on Friday suggested the US and European allies could give his country missiles they have stockpiled now , which would later be replenished by the new purchase. “We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” Zelenskyy said. People living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine were evacuated on Friday as part of a joint relief operation , the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war. The city, which lies on the Russian-occupied side of the Dnipro River has suffered months of food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation for the few thousand people remaining there, including children. A humanitarian convoy arrived in the city with food and medicine and to evacuate those wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine. It’s not clear how many people chose to evacuate but US first lady Melania Trump posted on social media on Friday that the convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Friday that as many as 20 million Ukrainians could be forced to flee to Europe if his country falls to Russia. “Russia is killing us,” Zelenskyy told reporters at a press conference on Friday during a summit of European Union leaders, adding Ukrainians were being “pushed” out of their country. “They [Russia] don’t want to stop.” In the early days of Russia’s full-scale invasion, millions of Ukrainians fled their homes in Europe’s fastest and largest refugee crisis since World War II. Today, over 4 million Ukrainians live in EU countries under temporary protection status, with the largest populations in Germany, Poland and Czechia, according to Eurostat . Zelenskyy’s stark warning comes as Ukraine heads into a brutal fifth wartime winter under Russian bombardment. Kyiv faces a budget shortfall of $30 to $35 million next year, according to projections from the International Monetary Fund — even accounting for a €90 billion loan Brussels agreed to provide last year.
